\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Routing in multimodal RAG is a scheduling decision over scarce GPU resources: generation grows with the request
rate, the visual index grows with the corpus, and interactive services are judged on tail latency. Measured end to
end with real retrieval and generation on one GPU, the content-aware router CAVR-CE uses 29\% less GPU compute
than always combining text and image contexts, at a mean ANLS cost of 0.008. In a load test simulated from
measured service times, it reduces the GPUs needed for 100 queries/s at p95 $\le$ 2\,s from 106 to
72. Its cost weight is set at serving time, and pre-generation escalation trades part of the
saving back for quality without adding a serial step. On a three-GPU node, sharding the visual index holds
exhaustive search at constant latency as the corpus grows with the number of GPUs, with parallel efficiency of at
least 99.6\% from 50k pages up.

The evaluation also corrects the earlier version of this work. Keyword-derived route labels do not reflect which path
answers correctly, list-price cost estimates do not survive measurement, and with a shared generator the text path is
not a cheap path. A per-query oracle (ANLS 0.630 at 0.486 GPU-s) shows how much remains: the
bottleneck is predicting, before generation, whether a path will succeed.

The routing results come from one GPU and simulated load, and sharding was measured on older GPUs for retrieval
only. Future work should validate routing on a multi-GPU cluster with a production serving engine, adapt $\lambda$ to measured load, improve per-query success
prediction, and extend routing to queries that contain images.
